title: Resistance and Resistivity
short: R = ρL/A, so longer and thinner wires resist more.
trouble: Students think a thicker wire has more resistance because there is more metal in it.

blocks.html: Ohm's law, $V = IR$, says how much voltage it takes to push a current through a resistance $R$. But what decides $R$? For a wire, three things: what it is made of, how long it is, and how thick it is.

Electrons drifting through a metal keep bumping into its vibrating atoms. A longer wire means more bumps along the way, like more resistors in a row: $R \propto L$. A thicker wire gives the electrons more paths side by side, like more resistors in parallel: $R \propto 1/A$. What is left depends on the material, its resistivity $\rho$. In most metals the atoms vibrate more when hot, so $\rho$ rises with temperature.
$$R = \rho\frac{L}{A}$$ with $\rho$ in $\Omega\cdot\text{m}$, $L$ in meters and $A$ in square meters. For a round wire, $A = \pi r^2 = \pi d^2/4$.

head: Material
$\rho$ near room temperature ($\Omega\cdot\text{m}$)
blocks.cap: Good conductors have tiny resistivities; insulators such as glass and rubber have resistivities trillions of times larger.

blocks.name: ph-circuit
blocks.cap: Two copper wires of the same length side by side: $R_1$ is the thick one, $R_2$ has half its diameter, so a quarter of the area and four times the resistance. The thin wire carries a quarter of the current.

blocks.title: A copper wire
blocks.q: Find the resistance of $20\,\text{m}$ of copper wire $1.0\,\text{mm}$ in diameter.

blocks.title: Scaling a wire
blocks.q: A wire has $R = 6.0\,\Omega$. Another of the same metal is twice as long with twice the diameter. Find its resistance.
steps: Twice the length doubles $R$. Twice the diameter gives four times the area, which divides $R$ by 4.

blocks.title: Sizing a heater element
blocks.q: How long must a nichrome wire ($\rho = 1.10 \times 10^{-6}\,\Omega\cdot\text{m}$) $0.40\,\text{mm}$ in diameter be to have $20\,\Omega$?

blocks.html: Thinking a thicker wire has more resistance because there is more metal in the way. The extra metal is extra path, side by side, not extra obstacle in a row. That is why thick cables are used for big currents. Check: $A$ is in the denominator of $\rho L/A$, so a bigger area means a smaller resistance.
